summary: Marketing site for a launched software product sold by subscription: a product-led home with a live or scripted demo, proof, features, setup steps and pricing, plus a pricing page, an optional integrations catalogue, a security / data-handling page and a release-notes page. Covers a general B2B app, a data / analytics product and an AI product through alternatives and optional sections.

pages.purpose: Show what the product does in the first screen (with the product itself, not stock art), prove it is used, explain the main jobs it does and get a trial or demo request.

sections.purpose: One line about the latest release that links to the release notes; shows the product is alive.
fields: One-line summary of what is new
sections.notes: Time-boxed: remove or update it when the release is more than a couple of months old.

sections.purpose: Promise in one line, who it is for, the two actions (start trial, see demo) and the product on screen.
alternatives: typing-demo: an AI or text product; a scripted rewrite (pick a situation and a tone, the result types out and lists what changed) sells better than a screenshot
area-chart: a data / analytics product; put a small live query console under the headline where metric, segment and range change the chart, the headline figures and the generated query together
media-text: the product is best shown as one large annotated screenshot
fields: Headline (one promise, the key word can be emphasised)
Lead: who it is for and the main outcome
Primary action (trial / sign-up) and its target
Secondary action (demo video or booked demo)
Product visual: a real screen or a recreated UI preview
Up to two headline figures with label (e.g. teams using it, median result), each with a source
Optional release tag linking to the release notes
sections.notes: Use the product hero variant with a visual of the actual product. For an interactive demo: build it from tabs / toggle groups, stat, sparkline and a chart; it must run on seeded demo data with no network calls, say so on screen, keep the key numbers as text in an aria-live region, and stop animating under reduced motion. Hero for a dark data product: headline above, console full width below.

sections.purpose: Show recognisable customers right under the hero.
fields: Caption saying where / by whom it is used
sections.notes: Marquee variant only with real logos and it must pause under reduced motion; a static row reads calmer for technical buyers.

sections.purpose: The three to five main jobs the product does, each with its own screen.
alternatives: tabs: when each feature needs a larger screenshot and the visitor should switch between them
description-list: a technical product that reads better as a dense capability sheet (index, name, one line, one measurable fact)
fields: Per feature: title, one or two sentences of what it does, screenshot or illustration
sections.notes: Tabs variant of feature-grid with one media per item; follow the tabs keyboard pattern.

sections.purpose: One concept that sets the product apart explained in depth (a metric layer, an alert feed, a before / after use case).
alternatives: activity-timeline: show a sample feed of alerts or events as the product would send them
comparison-table: before / after of the same task without and with the product
feature-grid: use cases as cards, each with the input people actually send and the result
fields: Problem it solves in plain words
Sample of what it produces (alert, rewrite, report) as text
Up to three small figures that back it up
sections.notes: Repeat for at most two concepts; samples must be clearly marked as examples.

sections.purpose: Measured results, each with where the number comes from.
fields: Per figure: value, unit, label, source (dataset or survey with sample size and period)
sections.notes: Never show a figure without a source line; counters may count up but must respect reduced motion.

sections.purpose: The smaller things buyers check for (seats, compliance, apps, integrations) in a dense grid.
fields: Per item: icon, title, one-line fact

sections.purpose: Where the product works or what it connects to, as a short teaser of the full list.
alternatives: feature-grid: integrations described as surfaces (email, docs, chat) without third-party logos
fields: Link to the full integrations page when there is one

sections.purpose: How fast a customer goes from sign-up to first result, as three or four timed steps.
fields: Per step: title, one sentence, time it takes

sections.purpose: Short answer to where data lives and who can see it, linking to the security page.
fields: Whether data is used to train models (AI products)
Compliance and agreements offered (DPA, KVKK, GDPR)

sections.purpose: One customer story (or a wall of short quotes for a technical audience) in their words.
Plans on the home page so visitors do not have to leave to compare.
fields: Plan names and who each is for
Price per plan and billing period (monthly / yearly)
Custom / sales-led plan and its contact action
Tax note and refund / cancellation footnote
sections.notes: On a multi-page site keep a short version here and link to the pricing page.

sections.purpose: Objections before buying: trial end, data location, setup requirements.
fields: Questions and answers buyers ask before signing up

sections.purpose: Repeat the main action at the end with the friction removed (no card, cancel any time).
fields: Phone / WhatsApp for sales when offered
sections.notes: Band variant on the accent surface.

pages.purpose: Let a buyer pick a plan and know the bill before talking to anyone.

sections.purpose: Page title and the one rule of the pricing (per seat, per location, per usage).
All plans with a monthly / yearly switch.
alternatives: page-pricing-01: a standard pricing page with plans, comparison and FAQ in one block
fields: Plan names, prices per billing period, included limits, highlighted plan, plan actions

sections.purpose: Usage-priced products: set seats and usage with sliders and see the monthly bill per plan, with the cheapest plan that fits marked.
fields: Pricing formula per plan (base, per seat, per usage unit)
sections.notes: Estimator with seat and usage sliders; the formula returns one line per plan, the cheapest that fits highlighted with a badge and plans that do not fit shown as text. The total is announced in a polite live region; show the formula in words under the result (notes).
alternatives: slider: two hand-built sliders beside a stat when only one figure changes

sections.purpose: Every feature line per plan for buyers who check details.
fields: Value or included / not per plan

sections.purpose: Billing questions: invoices, currency, VAT, plan changes, refunds.

pages.purpose: A searchable catalogue of what the product connects to, with honest status per connector.

sections.purpose: What connecting means (read-only, sync frequency) and how many connectors exist.
Filter by kind and status, search by name; each connector shows kind, sync method and status (available, beta, planned).
alternatives: data-table: a long technical list where sorting by column matters
fields: Per connector: name, kind, sync method / frequency, status, one-line note
sections.notes: Planned connectors must be labelled as planned (and hideable); show an empty state with a request action when nothing matches.

sections.purpose: Ask for a missing connector.

pages.purpose: Answer a buyer's security review on one page: data flow, retention, admin controls, subprocessors and how to report a vulnerability.

sections.purpose: Short promise about data handling with the key facts as meta.
sections.notes: A reading progress bar suits this long page.

sections.purpose: What happens to a piece of customer data from input to deletion, as steps.
fields: Steps of the data flow with what is stored where and for how long

sections.purpose: Retention per plan in a table.
Controls an admin can set (SSO, allowed domains, policy file).
fields: Admin controls and how they are configured

sections.purpose: Every third party that processes data, with purpose and region.
How to report a vulnerability and what the reporter can expect.
Remaining security questions.

pages.purpose: Release notes, newest first, so customers see the product moving and what changed for them.

sections.purpose: Release cadence and the latest version.
One block per release: version, date, title and the changes.
alternatives: feature-grid: few releases, each shown as a list of changes with icons
fields: Per release: version, ISO date, title, list of changes (title + one sentence)

sections.purpose: Turn a reader into a trial.

content: One-line promise and who the product is for
Real product screenshots or a recreated UI for the hero and each feature
For a demo: scripted demo inputs and results (AI) or seeded demo data (analytics), clearly marked as examples
Customer logos and quotes with written permission
Measured figures with source, sample size and period
Plans: names, prices per billing period, limits, tax note, refund and cancellation terms
Data handling facts: storage region, retention, model training policy, subprocessors, DPA
Release history with versions and dates
Trial and demo targets (sign-up URL, demo booking, sales contact)

styles.name: bright editorial glass
styles.why: A general B2B app sold to operators: friendly, with a cascading hero and a playing UI preview; quick motion keeps it lively.

styles.name: dense dark data
styles.why: Data, analytics and technical products: wide container, mono figures, hairline spec sheets; data people read specs, not slogans.

styles.name: dark AI glass
styles.why: AI products: dark by default with crisp short motion so the demo is the only thing that moves much.

pitfalls: Figures without a source ("38% fewer" with no survey, size or period) look invented; every stat needs a source line.
Demos that look like real customer data or make network calls; mark seeded / scripted data as an example and keep it local.
Interactive demos that only make sense visually: put the key numbers and the result in text and an aria-live region, honour reduced motion, keep controls keyboard reachable.
Prices shown without tax note, billing period or what happens at the end of the trial; yearly plans without refund terms.
Customer logos and quotes used without permission, or integration partner logos used against their brand rules.
AI products that do not say whether customer data trains models, where it is stored and who the subprocessors are.
Feature names in internal jargon; buyers search for the job ("shared inbox", "revenue dashboard"), not the module name.
A changelog that is not kept up: a stale announcement bar or last release from a year ago signals a dead product.
